title: Does 17th-century France matter in 21st-century Britain?
gist: Prospect's theatre critic compares two 2026 London adaptations of 17th-century French material: Martin Crimp's gender-flipped Misanthrope at the National Theatre with Sandra Oh as a cancelled post-feminist novelist, which she judges a failure of script development despite superb casting, and the RSC's Cyrano de Bergerac with Adrian Lester, which succeeds. The structural verdict is that Indhu Rubasingham's early National Theatre programme has invested in casting and costume at the expense of text.

themes.theme: Cancel-culture updating of Molière falls flat

insights.claim: Martin Crimp's 2026 National Theatre adaptation of The Misanthrope recasts Molière's Alceste as 'Alice', a post-feminist novelist cancelled from a Berlin festival for refusing to recant a specific word, transposing the play's attack on 'politesse' onto contemporary enforced political speech.
insights.speaker: Kate Maltby
insights.so_what: Documents how mainstream British institutional theatre is now directly dramatising speech-policing disputes rather than avoiding them.
insights.quote: we meet Sandra Oh as a gender-flipped Alceste, a post-feminist novelist who rails against cancel culture and refuses to limit her thinking to the niceties of left or right
insights.locator: In the opening of Martin Crimp’s new adaptation

insights.claim: Crimp's adaptation substitutes insider arts-world jokes for genuine analysis of the issues it raises, even recycling a Damien Hirst gag from his own 1996 version, and arrives at a resolution the critic calls risible.
insights.speaker: Kate Maltby
insights.so_what: A warning that topical framing does not substitute for dramatic structure — the production has star power but weak word of mouth.
insights.quote: Crimp spends more energy on inside jokes about the arts world than meaningful analysis of its issues.
insights.locator: Crimp spends more energy on inside jokes

insights.claim: The Misanthrope production undercuts its own verse by having Sandra Oh and her co-stars rattle off lines as casual patter, and a possible allusion to Gaza is swallowed in mumbling rather than delivered with conviction.
insights.speaker: Kate Maltby
insights.so_what: Directorial evasion on the most charged contemporary reference signals institutional caution at Britain's flagship subsidised theatre.
insights.quote: There might be an allusion to Gaza, but it is swallowed in mumbling

insights.claim: The RSC's Cyrano de Bergerac adaptation by Simon Evans and Debris Stevenson succeeds where The Misanthrope fails because it holds the balance between Rostand's emotional romance and his intellectual play with literary modes.
insights.speaker: Kate Maltby
insights.so_what: Identifies a repeatable formula for classical adaptation: preserve the emotional engine rather than only modernising the references.
insights.quote: Cyrano engages better with this material, in part because it maintains the balance between the emotional heft of Rostand’s central romance and the intellectual gamesmanship
insights.locator: Cyrano engages better with this material

insights.claim: Adrian Lester's Cyrano is performing at the height of his powers, out-writing Scott Handy's Comte de Guiche with complex sonnets and acrostics while duelling with the agility of a far younger man.
insights.speaker: Kate Maltby
insights.so_what: A career-peak lead performance in the West End is the kind of critical endorsement that drives extended runs and awards season attention.
insights.quote: Adrian Lester is at the height of his powers here, duelling across the stage with the agility of a far younger man
insights.locator: Adrian Lester is at the height of his powers

insights.claim: The Cyrano production gives Susannah Fielding's Roxanne licence to express rage at discovering that Cyrano's bro-code sense of honour destroyed their chance at love, a modern reframing that supplies the climax's tragic force.
insights.speaker: Kate Maltby
insights.so_what: Shows contemporary reinterpretation working when it changes a character's agency rather than merely updating topical references.
insights.quote: giving Susannah Fielding’s Roxanne licence to express a healthy sense of rage
insights.locator: Evans unleashes the production’s tragic impact

themes.theme: The libertine frame linking both plays

insights.claim: Both The Misanthrope and Cyrano de Bergerac are fundamentally plays about the power of literary form, asking whether language reveals or conceals us and whether language can be violence, and both centre a cynic whose cynicism masks romantic vulnerability.
insights.speaker: Kate Maltby
insights.so_what: A reusable critical lens for reading the current wave of speech-politics drama in British theatre.
insights.quote: Does language reveal or conceal us? Can language be violence?
insights.locator: Both Misanthrope and Cyrano are plays about power

insights.claim: 17th-century libertines like the historical Cyrano de Bergerac were dangerous because their disbelief in God led them to question the structures organising society, a link Crimp himself draws in his programme note.
insights.speaker: Kate Maltby
insights.so_what: Positions today's anti-consensus provocateurs in a long lineage, suggesting the cultural conflict is structural rather than novel.
insights.quote: Libertines – Cyrano de Bergerac being a well-known example – were dangerous because, not believing in God, they questioned the structures that organised society.
insights.locator: As Crimp acknowledges in his programme note

insights.claim: The Misanthrope is the latest disappointment in Indhu Rubasingham's early tenure as National Theatre artistic director, following The Bacchae, Hamlet and Les Liaisons Dangereuses, with the pattern being lavish costuming prioritised over script development.
insights.speaker: Kate Maltby
insights.so_what: A consistent critical pattern against a new artistic director at a flagship subsidised institution creates pressure on programming and funding narratives.
insights.quote: it would be nice to see a show at the National that has put more care put into script development than luxurious costuming
insights.locator: All newcomers to this job have had a rough start

insights.claim: Rubasingham's demonstrated strengths are creative commissioning, alchemical casting and reinvention of the classical canon, evidenced by The Wife of Willesden, Zadie Smith's version of Chaucer's Wife of Bath.
insights.speaker: Kate Maltby
insights.so_what: The critique is about execution on text, not capability — implying the National's programme is recoverable rather than structurally misdirected.
insights.quote: The Wife of Willesden, Zadie Smith’s version of Chaucer’s Wife of Bath, was her project, and will live with me as one of the best plays of the last decade.
insights.locator: All newcomers to this job have had a rough start
